title: No more rice grains in Kellogg's Rice Krispies due to changing weather
description: Breakfast cereal giant Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK due to "changing weather conditions" that have
body: Breakfast cereal giant Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies.Corn flour and rice flour are being used instead, a Kellogg's spokesperson said on Tuesday, adding that the updated recipes have been "carefully assessed" and the firm has taken customer feedback into consideration.Those ingredients are replacing rice grains as crops have been hit by dry weather in key producing countries in Asia, reducing harvests and driving up prices.The new recipes mean cereal packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning.Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada will continue to be made with real rice with no changes to their recipes expected, a spokesperson for Kellogg's North American business told the BBC.The recipe change in the UK will help "maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals," a Kellogg's spokesperson told the BBC."We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration."The company also said that Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.The cereals also contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same, the spokesperson added.

schema.headline: No more rice grains in Kellogg's Rice Krispies due to changing weather

title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial next month
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December,
body: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December, the BBC understands.The witness summons will see him giving evidence and taking questions, in a case in which a wealthy woman alleges she was cheated by her former financial adviser.Mountbatten-Windsor is not accused of wrongdoing, but he could face difficult questions about his financial arrangements as it is said that he was in receipt of some of the disputed payments, including a transfer to him of £750,000.His court appearance will be the first public questioning Mountbatten-Windsor has faced since his BBC Newsnight interview in 2019.It is also believed that Mountbatten-Windsor is the first royal since the 19th Century to be sent such a witness summons.Such an unusual royal moment is likely to receive widespread media coverage - not least for the opportunity to hear the former Duke of York's first public comments since being stripped of his titles.Last month, a judge gave permission for Mountbatten-Windsor to be called as a witness.The summons was issued this week, with the case set to begin from mid-November and with Mountbatten-Windsor to appear as a witness around the 15 December, which is usually in person, but could be on video.There have been many questions in recent years about Mountbatten-Windsor's personal finances - and challenges about a lack of transparency - and this case promises to give a rare opportunity to hear his own explanations about his financial dealings.The case will hear allegations made by Nebahat Isbilen, an elderly Turkish woman, who says her former adviser Selman Turk misled her and used her wealth to his own advantage.Turk has strongly denied dishonesty.Mountbatten-Windsor will be asked to give evidence related to disputed questions about the handling of Isbilen's money.According to court documents, Isbilen claimed she was misled by Turk into paying £750,000 to Mountbatten-Windsor, believing it was for help with a passport.Turk has denied the allegation and says this payment was a gift made on Isbilen's own initiative to create goodwill with the then duke and had nothing to do with a passport.The case covers payments made at the very end of his time as a working royal.The transfer of money came the day after Mountbatten-Windsor recorded his BBC Newsnight interview, which was then broadcast the following night, and was soon followed by the then Duke of York stepping down from royal duties.In 2021, Isbilen's lawyers contacted the then Prince Andrew and the money had been paid back, but the forthcoming court case will consider claims about Turk's behaviour, with Mountbatten-Windsor set to be a significant witness.Court documents show there will be questions about another significant sum of money paid from Isbilen's account - around £768,000 in January 2020.Turk has claimed it was a loan to Mountbatten-Windsor for the purchase of a chalet in Switzerland - a suggestion which is contested by Isbilen and had been challenged in previous court hearings.Turk had met Mountbatten-Windsor in autumn 2019 through the Pitch@Palace project, a Dragon's Den-style pitching event run by the former duke. That had led to social gatherings, bringing together Turk and his family, Isbilen and the then Duke and Duchess of York.Justice Adam Johnson has said that, given the seriousness of the allegations, Turk should have access to "the evidence he considers relevant and material".That meant that Turk wanted to use Mountbatten-Windsor's evidence and has been successful in summonsing him for that purpose.Turk's representatives, Janes Solicitors, said he denies the claims of dishonesty and looks forward to being vindicated in court.Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for a response.The trial at the High Court is expected to begin later this month.

schema.headline: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial next month

title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
description: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.The prime minister has said the UK will not pay reparations to affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.In 2007, Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret"."Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue." He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".Burnham now says the government is open to formally apologising for slavery. Ministers are beginning what they call a "structured dialogue" with affected countries, with the expectation that the apology may come at around the time the prime minister hosts the G20 Summit of world leaders in Manchester in November 2027."Is it weak to do this? I think it's the opposite of weak. I think fragile weak countries can't face up to their past. I'm really proud of Britain, but being proud of your country is also being willing to face up to things you didn't do, right?" Miliband said.He said he had asked to be provided with a historical digest of the UK's involvement in the slave trade."Over three million people shipped, really with the British state's complicity, over a long period of time, couple of centuries actually, hundreds of thousands of them didn't make it and died," the foreign secretary said."Those who did make it had appalling conditions. Reading about the conditions on the ships and what happened to them when they arrived in the Caribbean and the Americas is really pretty harrowing."Now he and the prime minister begin a process likely to formally apologise for this -and, they hope, create space for the Commonwealth to turn its attention to other things.

schema.headline: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers

title: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
description: Russian strikes on Ukraine – including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital – have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others ove
body: Russian strikes on Ukraine – including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital – have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof  collapsed, trapping many underneath. "The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen. However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment. According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital. But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law", external."I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad."These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating. The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting., externalThe UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities. At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

schema.headline: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital

title: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal
description: A celebrity who asked the High Court to permanently prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations of sexual misconduct h
body: A celebrity who asked the High Court to permanently prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations of sexual misconduct has lost his case, with the court saying the man's claim for an injunction was denied.But the judge said a temporary injunction preventing the man from being named and the allegations published should remain in place, in order to allow the celebrity to appeal against the judgment, with anonymity and reporting restrictions remaining in force during the period allowed for any appeal.ITN and the Guardian have said they believe it is in the public interest to publish allegations that the man abused his status to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".The man, who denies the allegations, said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.In his judgment on Tuesday, Mr Justice Nicklin rejected the injunction request.He said: "The court did not determine whether the allegations, or any of them, were true, and the dismissal of the claim does not amount to approval of any publication the defendants may decide to make."Nicklin noted that the man has repeatedly said he intends to take his own life if the allegations are published, and that this must be taken seriously.He added these statements do not "establish that suicide is inevitable or that treatment cannot reduce the risk".With a strict anonymity order remaining in place, it would be against the law to identify the man or publish details that might do so.The man can now take his case to the Court of Appeal. Sara Mansoori KC, representing the celebrity, asked the court for time to decide whether he wanted to challenge the ruling.She said that her client is "in a highly vulnerable position" and has "not been in a position to give us instructions on any appeal".The claimant must lodge reasons to appeal by 16:30 GMT on 9 November.The case raises highly unusual legal issues concerning whether a court should stop publication when an individual claims that a media investigation would lead to them inflicting harm on themselves.The celebrity first asked the court in the summer to stop the publication of the investigation after journalists contacted him with allegations about this sexual activities with a large number of young women.ITN and the Guardian said their investigation had uncovered how the celebrity had allegedly abused his "power and status".During last week's application for a permanent injunction, Mansoori said making the allegations public would have a "potentially fatal impact".The barrister told the court that the man had tried to kill himself after he had been contacted by the media organisations and was later detained in hospital for his own protection - but later absconded and tried a second time to end his life.Those incidents of self-harm had not been because of the allegations themselves but the result of "long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media", she argued."The only reason [suicide attempts] would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life," she said.Lawyers for the media groups argued that there was a strong public interest in allowing their investigation to be publicised because of the serious nature of the allegations.In his judgment, Nicklin wrote: "The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the conduct of a prominent person and the alleged  use of status, influence and access in dealings with women and girls."The subject matter includes alleged abuse of power, sexual misconduct and inappropriate conduct towards younger or vulnerable persons."Those are matters capable of making a significant contribution to public debate."The celebrity argued that publishing the allegations would breach his protections under the European Convention on Human Rights, including articles that guarantee the right to life and protection from inhuman or degrading treatment.However, the judge rejected the claim that publication would violate the man's right to life, writing: "No prior case establishes that the Court's knowledge of a suicide risk, together with its power to prohibit the event expected to increase that risk, is by itself enough to require the Court to act."The judge accepted that publishing would cause the man "acute and potentially prolonged mental suffering" – but said "established law did not impose a positive obligation upon the Court to prevent that suffering by restraining publication".The man also cited the right to private and family life.While the judge acknowledged that publication "would interfere exceptionally seriously with the Claimant's private and family life", he also rejected that claim, saying a permanent injunction "would have been an exceptionally serious restriction upon freedom of expression".The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

schema.headline: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal

title: Poundland supplier 'angry' with owners over administration
description: One of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses.While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small a
body: One of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses.While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small and medium-sized suppliers could go under.This is in addition to potentially thousands of job losses among staff.Politicians have been putting questions to representatives of Poundland owners Gordon Brothers this week seeking "clarity" on plans for the retailer.Adam Turner, sales director at Highcrest Retail Brands - a family owned Bradford business - told the BBC that Poundland was one of Highcrest's biggest customers, and that the firms have had a relationship for decades.Highcrest mainly sells confectionary to Poundland, and turns over about £50m.It will "lose a few million" if Poundland becomes insolvent, so it will have a gap in its balance sheet next year, he said.Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", but other medium and small suppliers have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they", Mr Turner said.This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.Not only 12,000 Poundland staff would be affected, but also potentially tens of thousands more, he said.If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present - meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.Mr Turner said that the last three months of the year is the "golden quarter" for retailers. In terms of sweets, Poundland will get its Halloween stock in from July, and Christmas stock in from September.These three months will be the time of year when suppliers will be owed the most by Poundland.If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" - although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit."It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years."It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.Mr Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations - selling off stock from collapsed businesses.One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" - most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.Meanwhile, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet with Gordon Brothers later this week after he and Prime Minister Andy Burnham questioned why a solvent deal had not been made.Business minster Kate Dearden told MPs that government officials had also met with representatives from Gordon Brothers on Monday."I am deeply concerned about the uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future and the impact it could have on its staff and their families who are at the forefront of my mind," Dearden told the House of Commons."Poundland is not currently in administration and the business continues to trade, but this is a worrying time for employees, suppliers and communities", she added.The minister confirmed she would also be meeting with Poundland executives on Wednesday.She said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but said ministers would be seeking "clarity" on the plans for the retailer."It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees, should the current situation end in administration."We stand ready to support them if they need to move into new employment, however... our priority is always in protecting jobs and the Secretary of State and I will continue to engage with the company to secure the best possible outcome," she added.The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland £85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.

schema.headline: Poundland supplier 'angry' with owners over administration

title: Democrat Jon Ossoff wins re-election to Senate in Georgia
description: FOLLOW LIVE - Election results and analysis RESULTS - Live US 2026 midterm results as they come in Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - could T
body: FOLLOW LIVE - Election results and analysis RESULTS - Live US 2026 midterm results as they come in Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - could Talarico turn the tide?News of Ossoff's projected victory, which was announced less than an hour after polls closed, rippled through the Georgia Democrats watch party in Atlanta with supporters cheering and clapping. He began his remarks by thanking his family and voters in Georgia for their support, replying "I love you, too", in response to shouts coming from the jubilant crowd.He returned to many of the points he made on the campaign trail, expressing his concern about the economic woes faced by everyday Americans, while attacking big pharma and corporate America and alleged corruption in the White House."This moment is an opening not for restoration, but for reformation," Ossoff said. "And so, amidst our celebration tonight, we must acknowledge that the underlying crisis gripping our Republic remains, and that therefore, our most vital work lies ahead."The race was one of the first major contests projected as part of the midterms on Tuesday, which will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome will determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.Brian Kemp, Georgia's term-limited Republican governor, was the favoured candidate to run against Ossoff, but he declined. Political pundits suspected that Kemp had avoided running, wary of Ossoff's rising star power, with rumours swirling that the Democrat could be mulling a run for president in 2028.Throughout his campaign, Ossoff downplayed such rumours, saying on multiple occasions that he has "zero interest" in a presidential bid. His messaging on the campaign trail focused on the economy and voter concerns around affordability, which exit polls show was the top issue for many.

schema.headline: Democrat Jon Ossoff wins re-election to Senate in Georgia

title: Killer who escaped Tennessee prison captured after week-long manhunt
description: Figure caption, Officials say this video shows escaped inmate stealing a truckByHelen DavidsonUS authorities have recaptured a convicted murderer who
body: Figure caption, Officials say this video shows escaped inmate stealing a truckByHelen DavidsonUS authorities have recaptured a convicted murderer who escaped a Tennessee prison more than a week ago.Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence over the killing of his colleague in 2022, when he escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis.The Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) said security footage showed Morley, wearing his prison uniform, breaching the prison fence around 11:30pm on 25 October, and later stealing a vehicle from a nearby farm.On Wednesday the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) announced Morley was in custody after an operation that involved local, state and federal agencies.In a statement, the TBI said authorities had received a tip that Morley was hiding on an Illinois property, from which a truck had also been stolen. The truck's licence plate was then tracked through automatic plate-reader technology, travelling through Missouri, where local authorities were dispatched to follow.Morley was apprehended by Missouri State Highway Patrol "without incident" in Carroll County at 11:34am local time on Tuesday. Three firearms that had previously been reported stolen were also recovered from the vehicle, the TBI said.Photos published by authorities showed Morley handcuffed and being led out of a field by officers.Image source, Missouri State Highway PatrolImage caption, Morley was apprehended by officers in MissouriFollowing his escape, Morley had been added to the TBI's most wanted list, with the TDOC offering a reward of up to $2,500 (£1,900) for information leading to his arrest. The reward was increased by $15,000 on Wednesday.The TBI's statement said members of the public had provided information during the investigation, but did not say if the reward had been paid.The Missouri State Highway Patrol said the manhunt had involved officers from the Kansas City Police Department, Independence Police Department, the FBI, US Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations.Image source, Tennessee Department of CorrectionImage caption, Morley was convicted of first-degree murder over the killing of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022Morley was convicted of first-degree murder over the death of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022. He was sentenced in June 2025. His request for a new trial was denied in May.Birchfield's body was found in a metal box under Morley's home, according to Carter County court records reviewed by the BBC. Birchfield died "as a result of a gunshot wound to the back of the head", a pathology report cited in court said. Bullet casings matched a gun found in Morley's house.Birchfield's sister said in her victim impact statement to the court that the pair had developed a friendship while Birchfield was training Morley at the pallet manufacturing company where they were both employed.Besides murder, Morley was also convicted of vandalism, tampering with evidence, aggravated burglary, and evading arrest.This is not the first time Morley has led law enforcement officials on a manhunt. His 2022 arrest came after a police chase that crossed state lines into North Carolina.The Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold up to 1,776 inmates, from low security to maximum, the BBC's partner CBS reported. CBS said the prison has seen numerous acts of violence in recent years, and in July a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over assaults on staff and the murders of five inmates.

schema.headline: Killer who escaped Tennessee prison captured after week-long manhunt

title: Young NYC Marathon runner collapses and dies two miles from finish line
description: A 24-year-old runner in the New York City Marathon collapsed and died just two miles from the finish line, despite being in "perfect health, perfect s
body: A 24-year-old runner in the New York City Marathon collapsed and died just two miles from the finish line, despite being in "perfect health, perfect shape", her father has said. Rachel Apa, from Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was running on Sunday with the Parkinson's Foundation Champions to raise money and honor her grandfather who had the disease, she said in a fundraising page. It was Apa's first marathon, though she was an athlete and had trained for months, father Steve Apa told the New York Times.She died from rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition where muscles break down and poison the bloodstream, which can be brought on by overexertion, her father said.Near mile marker 24, Apa collapsed in Central Park and a bystander performed CPR before race medical staff arrived, race organiser New York Road Runners told the BBC's US partner CBS News. According to a New York Police Department statement, which did not name Apa, she was taken to hospital in critical condition.She died that night. The city medical examiner's office said it is still investigating Apa's cause of death. Around Mile 18, the Times reported that Apa had texted her father "Ow" and then a mile later "Ow ow", before sending the message "final stretch" at the 23rd mile, according to the Times. "We are deeply saddened by Rachel's passing following running in Sunday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends, and the entire running community," New York Road Runners said in a statement obtained by CBS.Apa graduated with a business degree in 2024 from Pennsylvania's Bucknell University, where she also played field hockey, according to her LinkedIn profile online. Since graduating, she had worked as a product manager at an industrial technology company. Ahead of the race, Apa wrote on her marathon fundraising page how much her grandfather, who she was honoring with the run meant to her.  "My grandfather was my role model growing up," she wrote. "He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement."She said he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. "I watched as the disease slowly took away the freedom to move that he once loved so much," she continued. "The lessons he taught me continue to drive me forward."More than 61,000 people participated in this year's New York City Marathon, which for the third year in a row broke the world's record for largest marathon.

schema.headline: Young NYC Marathon runner collapses and dies two miles from finish line

title: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
description: Puente announced his decision at the end of a lengthy congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and h
body: Puente announced his decision at the end of a lengthy congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and had been grilled by the opposition. He also said: "I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but... I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections."Puente's position immediately came under scrutiny after the 28 October crash. The main opposition, the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox, were both calling for his resignation - as were some of the government's allies. They argued that the minister should take responsibility for a high-speed rail system that many Spaniards now regard as unsafe and whose credibility even Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez admitted was "broken".The opposition also criticised Puente for appearing to blame human error for the crash, claiming the minister was trying to deflect the blame from his own failings.But, having said he was going to remain in his post just a few days ago, his resignation appears to have taken many by surprise.The rail accident and Puente's decision have come at a crucial moment in the Spanish political calendar, with early general elections on 29 November.Many observers see the accident as a massive electoral setback to the Socialist-led government that will make it impossible for Sánchez to defy the polls and win the election. Puente's predicament presented him and the prime minister with a dilemma - refusing to resign might look insensitive in the wake of the accident and stepping down could look like acknowledging he and the government were at fault.In the end, Puente opted for the second option, insisting his decision had been driven by "political dignity".The prime minister praised his colleague who had "faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside". "Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims," Sánchez added. Many Spaniards will now ask whether Puente's successors will manage to restore faith in the country's railway system.In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties. After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.

schema.headline: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash

title: Democrats push deep into Republican territory with historic midterms wins
description: This is already shaping up to be a historic night for Democrats, with the party winning control of US House of Representatives and on their way to fli
body: This is already shaping up to be a historic night for Democrats, with the party winning control of US House of Representatives and on their way to flipping the Senate, too.The Democrats notched their first shock win in the Senate, when Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds have turned out to be slam dunks for the Democrats - Jon Ossoff's re-election in Georgia and the open Republican-held seat in North Carolina.That North Carolina contest, where former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper bested Republican Party insider Michael Whatley, was the first of the four pick-ups Democrats need in order to wrest control of the Senate. With South Carolina in the bag, they are halfway home.Attention has now turned to vote counts in Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and Ohio.US midterm elections results 2026Live updatesThe BBC's US partner CBS News is rating the Texas and Kansas Senate races as leaning Democrat. The governor's race in Texas, where just last year incumbent Republican Greg Abbott was a prohibitive favourite, is now considered a toss-up.Meanwhile, the Democrats have won a House majority for the first time since 2022.A look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.In Florida, Republicans in the state legislature had redrawn the boundaries of three Democratic-held seats to make it much easier to for them to win.They lost all three.Other House races in the state, where Republicans expected to win by comfortable margins, have turned out to be dogfights.Democrats flipped open seats in western North Carolina and Kentucky, for instance, and appear well placed to make gains in Virginia and Indiana.They're doing it on the back of high Democratic turnout, particularly by black voters in the south, and winning back Hispanic voters in Florida who had supported the Republicans just two years ago.In majority black South Carolina counties, Democratic Senate candidate Andrews significantly outperformed Kamala Harris's presidential numbers in 2024.And in Miami-Dade County, which Trump carried that year, Democratic candidates are back on top.If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds in his bid for governor. But the Sunshine State may prove to be one of the few bright spots.While the mood of the electorate appears to have turned against President Donald Trump and Republicans across the board, the US is a vast nation with unique geographic and demographic characteristics.A good night for Democrats in the east does not necessarily translate to similar performance across the country. But early results from America's heartland seem to be following the east-coast trend.A Democratic wave has formed on the horizon. Now it's just a question of exactly how far it crashes into Republican terrain.

schema.headline: Democrats push deep into Republican territory with historic midterms wins

title: Code cracked for Margam shipwreck padlock solving 400-year-old mystery
description: Image source, Amgueddfa CymruImage caption, The brass lock was discovered off the Welsh coast and dates back to 1583ByMeleri WilliamsBBC WalesExperts
body: Image source, Amgueddfa CymruImage caption, The brass lock was discovered off the Welsh coast and dates back to 1583ByMeleri WilliamsBBC WalesExperts have cracked a four-letter code to open an ancient padlock from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast using modern scanning technology.The 400-year-old brass lock was discovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes in the sand near Margam in Port Talbot, in 1999.It forms part of a wider treasure hoard from the Ann Francis ship that was caught in a storm on 28 December 1583 on the way back from Spain. Its cargo was hidden beneath the sand for centuries.Museum experts have used CT scanning to examine the lock's internal mechanism, identify the correct letter combination and solve the mystery.Image caption, Peter Hughes found the lock, along with coins and other artefacts, while walking with his metal detectorPeter Hughes, from Maesteg, said the padlock was one of hundreds of artefacts he found after decades of searching on Morfa beach.Found near a collection of Spanish silver coins and close to two coin weights, it is thought the lock may have protected these objects or secured a chest containing valuable items that did not survive, like documents or textiles."It was by chance - a day off. I was walking along the beach with my metal detector on a day off, and I came across a coin," the 69-year-old said."That was the start of a journey that lasted 21 years."Image caption, The code spells out ANCE and the inside resembles a keyHe said he was "delighted" that the expert team at Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University cracked the padlock code after he spent years trying to solve the mystery himself."I tried to unlock it for about 20 years, I tried moving the dials, finding the right combinations, and I failed," he said."But with the aid of modern technology we've been able to crack what's like the Da Vinci code, really."For me, it's like opening the Ark of the Covenant, and I'm delighted, truly thrilled."'Cracking the code was like a puzzle'Dr David Williams, a research associate based at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said he was "sceptical" when he was asked to use a scanning device to try and solve the mystery."It's challenging, the device we have is not designed to this particular purpose," he said."This is micro CT scanning, something you'd get at the hospital, but for smaller items."Williams said he was "always open to a challenge" and trying to "figure out a puzzle"."We did a first scan to see if we could see anything and we were quite surprised that we could see letters," he said."The second scan went terribly, but with the third scan, we tried a different approach, and figured out the code."I was blown away that we actually cracked it."Image caption, Senior curator Alastair Willis said the unlocking was complexHughes passed on the hoard of artefacts to Amgueddfa Cymru in 2017, and the collection, with the lock in the centre, was put on display at Swansea Waterfront Museum in July 2026.Senior curator Alastair Willis said the discovery of the code, which spells out ANCE, was "incredible"."It's really complex because there are so many combinations," he said."There are four different rings, and because there are six different letters on each of the rings, there are 1,296 different combinations, and you have to make sure they're aligned with the loop at the top."Image caption, Siân Iles works as a senior curator with Amgueddfa Cymru and said the team were "intrigued" with the brass lockHis colleague at Amgueddfa Cymru, senior curator Siân Iles, said the lock was in "excellent condition" and paints a picture of the period."This is a wonderful example of one that still functions as it would have done hundreds of years ago," she said."Because it was found so close to the wreck of the Ann Francis and with all the material that's part of that collection, it provides a really good context, it allows us to really tightly date it."I've seen others, and they're usually corroded and in different parts, but it was in wonderful condition."It's a small object so it probably would have been a lock for a chest or a small box, we don't know the content, and that's part of the story, there are some things we'll never know, but it's something that would have meant something to the person who knew that code."What should you do if you discover treasure?Treasure has a variety of definitions, external, as per the Treasure Act of 1996.In Wales, if you find treasure it must be reported to a Finds Liaison Officer, external within 14 days of first finding it or within 14 days of realising an item might be treasure, even if you have had it for longer.Only items officially defined as treasure need to be reported and there is a fine or up to three months in prison for not reporting.There are different rules for Scotland, external and Northern Ireland, external.After a find is reported, you will be contacted by either a Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator to talk about how and where you made the find. The Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator will then write a report on the find and the coroner will hold an inquest. The Finds Liaison Officer will help you get the coins assessed by experts to determine if they meet the legal definition of "treasure" under the Treasure Act 1996, external.If a museum wants the treasure, the Treasure Valuation Committee will ask an expert to value the find.They will recommend to the Secretary of State for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, external how much the treasure is worth and how much should go to anyone eligible for a share of a reward.

schema.headline: Code cracked for Margam shipwreck padlock solving 400-year-old mystery

title: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges
description: Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.The
body: Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date."That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments  disconnected from the internet.Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited. But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries"."We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said."We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing"."There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?""In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts."Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium. Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected."At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added. "We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

schema.headline: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges

title: Prince William says climate change makes UK wildfire risk terrifying
description: There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.
body: There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives."We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black."You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building."I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes."You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."

schema.headline: Prince William says climate change makes UK wildfire risk terrifying
